opening.argument: The presentation links concrete rewards to actions that viewers must take. It advertises unlimited free movies, songs, and coupons only after downloading and installing an OfferA2Z plug-in, and presents a free smartphone after buying cosmetics for 25 USD and installing that same plug-in. That is not merely discussion of advertising: the promised assets are explicitly conditioned on installation, with the smartphone additionally conditioned on a purchase. The combination creates a direct acquisition pathway in which the viewer is asked to install software, and in one case spend money, to obtain something advertised as free.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material a service promotion does not resolve the specific reward solicitation. The reference statement emphasizes call-generation services and training, but the presentation also places installation-linked free movies, coupons, and a smartphone in front of viewers. Those offers are concrete action-and-reward claims, not merely evidence that a business sells campaign setup.

opening.argument: Several unusually attractive claims are presented together with external acquisition steps. The material shows free HD movies, songs, and coupons tied to downloading and installing a plug-in, plus a smartphone advertised as absolutely free after a cosmetics purchase and another installation. It also promotes free offers, loans, and credits through a search site and invites viewers to join WhatsApp for a free demo. This combination of easy rewards, a required download, a purchase condition, and off-platform contact is a substantial warning pattern: the apparent benefit is used to move viewers toward software installation, spending, or direct contact.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening treats the risky tactics as incidental to an ordinary service, but the slides make them central to the advertised traffic model. They describe adware, browser or system freezing popups, and calls generated through injection processes, while the separate reward examples add installation and purchase hooks. A disclaimer or service framing does not make those combined solicitation signals ordinary.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Red flags are not proof of a scam. The slides can be read as examples of ad placements offered through a marketing service, and the evidence does not show that the advertised rewards were false, that a download caused harm, or that contact led to a deceptive transaction. Even the pop-up language establishes an aggressive advertising method, not a completed victim interaction.

opening.argument: The apparent instructional or ordinary-commerce framing functions as a solicitation. The title offers to generate inbound tech-support popup calls and supplies a Skype contact, while the description advertises adware solutions, campaign setup, training, and calls generated through paid campaigns. The presentation then supplies a free-demo invitation and contact channels, alongside free-reward advertisements that require installation or purchase. Taken together, this is promotional steering: viewers are directed toward contacting the provider, adopting the promoted software process, and pursuing offers whose benefits depend on further action.
